---
title: "StyleGAN, Normalization, Attention, and Image Translation"
---

## Overview {#sec-overview}

Earlier GAN lectures asked how a discriminator measures mismatch between real and generated distributions. This lecture asks a different question: **where should a generator receive information so that we can control what it generates?** The lecture moves from feature normalization and attention, through StyleGAN and content-style disentanglement, to paired, unpaired, and multi-domain image translation. The organizing equation is $Y=AXT+B$: left multiplication acts on spatial positions, while right multiplication acts on channels.

The main exposition follows *Part 1 - GAN*, pp. 78--125, and the accompanying lecture transcript [@lecture-slides; @lecture-script]. Paper-level equations are added where they clarify a model discussed in class. A section of advanced topics at the end collects the material that was not developed in the provided pp. 78--125/script, so that the main narrative follows the class itself.

**Color key.** $\textcolor{blue}{\text{Blue}}$ marks spatial/content control; $\textcolor{red}{\text{red}}$ marks style/channel control; $\textcolor{violet}{\text{violet}}$ marks reconstruction or consistency; $\textcolor{teal}{\text{teal}}$ marks domain supervision; and $\textcolor{orange}{\text{orange}}$ marks diversity. Shared adversarial terms remain black. Labels accompany color so that the comparisons remain readable in grayscale.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| $N=HW$, $C$, $M$ | Spatial positions, feature channels, and minibatch size |
| $X=[x_1,\ldots,x_C]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}$ | One image's feature matrix; $x_c$ is a spatial channel map |
| $x^n\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times C}$ | Row of $X$: channel features at position $n$ |
| $\mathbf 1_N$, $I_N$, $\operatorname{diag}(v)$ | All-ones vector, identity matrix, diagonal matrix |
| $\mu_X$, $\Sigma_X$ | Channel mean vector and centered channel covariance |
| $x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}}$, $y\sim p_{\mathcal{Y}}$ | Images from two domains, distinct from feature matrix $X$ |
| $G$, $F$, $D$ | Generators and discriminator; each section states their domains |
| $z$, $w$, $s$ | Prior latent, mapped latent, and style code |
| $k$, $t$, $K$ | Source domain, target domain, number of domains |
| $T_\#p$ | Push-forward: the distribution of $T(u)$ when $u\sim p$ |

Unless stated otherwise, expectations are over the displayed data and independently sampled latent variables. Empirical variances use divisor $N$, not $N-1$, matching the lecture. Formulas assume positive variances; implementations add $\epsilon>0$ under square roots. Norm subscripts distinguish the vector $L_1/L_2$ norms from the matrix Frobenius norm $\|\cdot\|_F$.

## Normalization as channel-wise transformation {#sec-normalization}

### What is averaged in batch, layer, and instance normalization?

For a minibatch tensor $X_{mnc}$, normalization has the common form

$$
Y_{mnc}=\gamma\frac{X_{mnc}-\mu}{\sqrt{v+\epsilon}}+\beta.
$$ {#eq-normalization}

The important difference is not this formula, but which entries share its statistics. The following table uses the **CNN layer-normalization convention on slide 87**, which pools spatial positions and channels within one image [@lecture-slides, pp. 83--88; @batchnorm; @layernorm; @instancenorm].

| Method | Mean; variance uses the same averaging set | Shared over | Main benefit / limitation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Batch normalization (BN) | $\mu_c=\frac{1}{MN}\sum_{m,n}X_{mnc}$ | Batch and positions, separately per channel | Useful optimization conditioning; batch-dependent estimates and train/test statistics can differ |
| Layer normalization (LN) | $\mu_m=\frac{1}{NC}\sum_{n,c}X_{mnc}$ | All features of one image | Independent of batch size; this choice does not standardize each channel separately |
| Instance normalization (IN) | $\mu_{mc}=\frac1N\sum_nX_{mnc}$ | Positions of one image and channel | Removes per-image channel contrast; may discard useful absolute intensity information |

For each table row, $v$ is the average of $(X-\mu)^2$ over the indicated indices. BN and IN use channel-specific learned $\gamma_c,\beta_c$. Slide 87 simplifies LN to shared scalar gain and bias; the original LN paper also allows neuron-wise gains and biases. Transformer token-wise LN is another axis choice: it normalizes channels within each token, not all positions in an image. These choices should not be silently interchanged.

![The difference between batch, layer and instance normalization. Each cube is a feature tensor with batch axis $N$, channel axis $C$ and spatial axes $(H,W)$; the shaded entries are the ones that share a mean and a standard deviation. Adapted from [@groupnorm, Fig. 2], with the group-normalization panel omitted.](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-norm-methods.png){#fig-norm-methods width=100%}

BN uses minibatch statistics during training and population estimates at inference. IN recomputes statistics separately for each image; LN also avoids dependence on other minibatch samples. The transcript initially describes BN statistics as channel-independent but then explicitly corrects this: $\mu_c$ and $v_c$ depend on the channel [@lecture-script].

### Deriving the matrix representation

Suppress the batch index. Set $\sigma_c=\sqrt{v_c+\epsilon}$, $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_C)^\top$, and $\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_C)^\top$. Expanding each normalized channel gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_c&=\frac{\gamma_c}{\sigma_c}x_c+
\left(\beta_c-\frac{\gamma_c\mu_c}{\sigma_c}\right)\mathbf1_N,\\
Y&=X\,\textcolor{red}{T}+B,\\
T&=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_1/\sigma_1,\ldots,\gamma_C/\sigma_C),\qquad
B=\mathbf1_N(\beta^\top-\mu^\top T).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-norm-matrix}

This is the lecture's $Y=XT+B$ representation. A diagonal $T$ rescales channels; a dense $T$ can mix them. Neither directly routes a value from one spatial position to another. For IN the matrices depend on the current image; for BN they also depend on the minibatch. Thus this is **an affine representation conditional on the computed statistics**, not a claim that the complete normalization operation is a fixed affine function of $X$.

## Style transfer: statistics, AdaIN, and transport {#sec-style-transfer}

### Adaptive instance normalization

For content features $X$ and reference-style features $S$, AdaIN replaces learned fixed IN gains and biases by reference statistics [@adain, Secs. 3--4; @lecture-slides, pp. 80, 89--90]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{AdaIN}(x_c,s_c)
&=\textcolor{red}{\sigma_{S,c}}\,
\frac{x_c-\mu_{X,c}\mathbf1_N}{\sigma_{X,c}}
+\textcolor{red}{\mu_{S,c}}\mathbf1_N,\\
Y&=(X-\mathbf1_N\mu_X^\top)
\textcolor{red}{D_X^{-1}D_S}+\mathbf1_N\mu_S^\top,
\quad D_X=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_X).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-adain-def}

$D_S$ is defined similarly; $X$ and $S$ need not have the same number of positions. A fixed encoder, this transform, and a learned decoder produce a stylized image. The decoder is trained using content-feature and style-statistic losses. Reference statistics are computed from $S$, not new free parameters trained for every reference image.

![The feed-forward style transfer network of @sec-adv-adain-training. A fixed VGG encoder maps the content and style images to feature space, AdaIN aligns the channel-wise statistics of the content features with those of the style features, and a learned decoder maps the result back to an image. The same encoder computes the content loss $\mathcal{L}_c$ and the style loss $\mathcal{L}_s$ used to train the decoder. Adapted from [@adain, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-adain-arch.png){#fig-adain-arch width=100%}

**Advantage:** efficient arbitrary-reference stylization without an eigendecomposition. **Limitation:** channel means and variances do not determine cross-channel covariance or a general feature distribution. A successful feature transform also need not invert perfectly through the decoder.

### Why AdaIN resembles Gaussian optimal transport

The lecture connects AdaIN to Gaussian optimal transport [@lecture-slides, pp. 40, 80; @lecture-script]. Here is the missing one-dimensional derivation. Let $U\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_u,\sigma_u^2)$ and $V\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_v,\sigma_v^2)$, with positive standard deviations. For squared Euclidean transport cost, the increasing quantile map is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T(u)
&=F_V^{-1}(F_U(u))\\
&=\mu_v+\sigma_v\Phi^{-1}\left(\Phi\left(\frac{u-\mu_u}{\sigma_u}\right)\right)\\
&=\mu_v+\frac{\sigma_v}{\sigma_u}(u-\mu_u).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-gaussian-ot}

$\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. Consequently, $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal T(U)]=\mu_v$ and $\operatorname{Var}[\mathcal T(U)]=\sigma_v^2$. For Gaussian channel vectors with **diagonal covariance** and separable squared cost, applying this map coordinate-wise gives AdaIN. The channels may have different means and variances: independence, rather than identical distributions across channels, is the relevant condition.

For positive-definite full covariances, the Gaussian squared-cost map for column vectors is instead

$$
\mathcal T(u)=\mu_S+M(u-\mu_X),\quad
M=\Sigma_X^{-1/2}
(\Sigma_X^{1/2}\Sigma_S\Sigma_X^{1/2})^{1/2}
\Sigma_X^{-1/2}.
$$ {#eq-full-gaussian-ot}

Thus the lecture's OT interpretation is exact under a Gaussian/diagonal model, not a theorem that empirical CNN features are Gaussian or that AdaIN transports their complete non-Gaussian distributions optimally.

### Whitening and coloring transform

WCT extends channel-wise scaling to full channel covariance [@wct, Sec. 3.2; @lecture-slides, p. 91]. With $X_c=X-\mathbf1_N\mu_X^\top$ and $\Sigma_X=X_c^\top X_c/N$, write $\Sigma_X=U_X\Lambda_XU_X^\top$ and similarly for $S$. In the lecture's row-vector convention,

$$
Y=X_c\,\textcolor{red}{\Sigma_X^{-1/2}\Sigma_S^{1/2}}
+\mathbf1_N\mu_S^\top.
$$ {#eq-wct}

The covariance calculation makes the two steps explicit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(X_c\Sigma_X^{-1/2})&=I_C,\\
\operatorname{Cov}(Y)&=
\Sigma_S^{1/2}\Sigma_X^{-1/2}\Sigma_X\Sigma_X^{-1/2}\Sigma_S^{1/2}
=\Sigma_S.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-wct-cov}

**Advantage:** matches correlations that diagonal AdaIN ignores. **Limitation:** forming a covariance costs $O(NC^2)$ and a dense eigendecomposition costs $O(C^3)$; small eigenvalues need regularization or truncation. Exact full-rank matching assumes positive-definite covariances.

**Clarification of the slide:** the covariance is centered and the mean correction is $B=\mathbf1_N\mu_S^\top-\mathbf1_N\mu_X^\top T$, not a channel-wise diagonal expression copied unchanged from AdaIN. WCT is a valid covariance-matching transport, but it is generally not the squared-cost optimal map in @eq-full-gaussian-ot. They coincide in the diagonal, or more generally commuting-covariance, case.

## Attention: transformation along the other axis {#sec-attention}

### Queries, keys, and values

A spatial attention layer combines rows rather than columns. A query represents what an output position seeks, a key supplies matching information, and a value is the information to be aggregated. With $W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d}$ and $W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d_v}$, set $Q=XW_Q$, $K=XW_K$, and $V=XW_V$. The output is [@lecture-slides, pp. 92--95; @attention]

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{mn}&=\frac{\exp(\operatorname{score}(q^m,k^n))}
{\sum_{j=1}^N\exp(\operatorname{score}(q^m,k^j))},\\
y^m&=\sum_{n=1}^Na_{mn}v^n,\qquad
Y=\textcolor{blue}{A}XW_V.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-attention}

The lecture lists dot-product, scaled dot-product, and cosine scores:

$$
qk^\top,\qquad \frac{qk^\top}{\sqrt d},\qquad
\frac{qk^\top}{\|q\|_2\|k\|_2}.
$$

For a fixed query index $m$, $\sum_na_{mn}=1$: **rows of $A$ sum to one**. The exponential normalization is softmax, not the sigmoid mentioned hesitantly in the transcript. $W_Q,W_K,W_V$ are learned linear projections; the attention layer becomes nonlinear through its data-dependent weights. In cross-attention, queries and key/value features can come from different inputs, giving a generally rectangular $A$.

**Advantage:** dense attention provides direct long-range interaction. **Limitation:** explicitly forming self-attention requires $O(N^2)$ weights; that cost grows rapidly with image resolution. The value projection changes the channel representation, but does not itself standardize a mean or variance.

### The unified transform and its limits

The lecture collects these operations as

$$
\boxed{Y=\underbrace{\textcolor{blue}{A}}_{\text{spatial axis}}
X\underbrace{\textcolor{red}{T}}_{\text{channel axis}}+B.}
$$ {#eq-unified}

At index level, $Y_{nc}=\sum_{m,j}A_{nm}X_{mj}T_{jc}+B_{nc}$. This immediately distinguishes dense spatial mixing, diagonal spatial gating, and channel mixing. In @fig-axes, each row isolates one selected output row or channel so the action of $A$ or $T$ is visually unambiguous.

![Illustration of how left and right multiplication act on different indices in $Y=AXT+B$; $B$ is omitted for clarity. Each row visualizes one selected output row or one selected output channel. Dense spatial attention mixes many input positions into one output position, diagonal spatial attention gates a position without within-layer position mixing, and diagonal channel modulation rescales one channel across all positions.](figures/lec03/Jeongchan-Kim-axes.png){#fig-axes width=100%}

The lecturer's word *dual* describes complementary tensor axes, not optimization duality. For fixed $T$, $\operatorname{col}(XT)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(X)$; for fixed $A$, $\operatorname{row}(AX)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(X)$. However, statistics-dependent $A,T,B$ must be recomputed when their inputs change. Associativity $(AX)T=A(XT)$ for fixed matrices does **not** imply that complete normalization and attention layers commute, or that separate axes guarantee independent semantic factors.

## Generators with style and content control {#sec-generators}

Here *disentanglement* means being able to vary one designated group of attributes while holding another approximately fixed. The lecture associates content with pose, geometry, and expression, and style with appearance and sometimes identity [@lecture-slides, pp. 104--113]. This is an operational convention, not a universal taxonomy.

### StyleGAN: learned styles and stochastic detail

StyleGAN starts from a **learned** $4\times4\times512$ constant tensor shared across generated samples. An eight-layer mapping MLP produces $w=f(z)\in\mathcal{W}$ from $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; layer-specific affine maps produce style parameters [@stylegan, Secs. 2--3; @lecture-slides, pp. 79, 101--103]. A synthesis stage can be summarized as

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_\ell&=\operatorname{Conv}_\ell(\operatorname{Up}(X_{\ell-1})),\\
u_{\ell c}&=\rho(h_{\ell c}+\textcolor{blue}{b_{\ell c}n_\ell}+a_{\ell c}),\\
X_{\ell c}&=\textcolor{red}{\gamma_{\ell c}(w)}
\frac{u_{\ell c}-\mu(u_{\ell c})}{\sigma(u_{\ell c})}
+\textcolor{red}{\beta_{\ell c}(w)},
\qquad (\gamma_\ell,\beta_\ell)=L_\ell(w).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-stylegan}

Here $n_\ell$ is a spatial Gaussian noise map shared across channels with learned channel scales $b_{\ell c}$; $\rho$ is the nonlinearity. Upsampling is omitted at layers that retain resolution. Unlike reference-based AdaIN, style parameters are predicted from $w$; a predicted gain need not be a positive reference standard deviation.

Why use $\mathcal{W}$? The mapping can reshape the simple prior before synthesis, rather than forcing all semantic variation to follow its geometry directly. The paper measures improved disentanglement using perceptual path length and linear separability; this is empirical, not guaranteed. Style mixing uses different $w$ values before and after a selected layer. Resampling noise mainly changes stochastic detail, not a controlled semantic attribute.

**Advantage:** scale-specific control with high-resolution synthesis. **Limitation:** styles can still change pose and geometry, so *style* is broader than texture; complete content-style separation is absent. Its contribution is architectural, not a new GAN divergence.

![A traditional generator (left) feeds the latent code $z$ through its input layer only. The style-based generator of StyleGAN (right) maps $z$ to $w$ with the mapping network $f$, feeds $w$ to every AdaIN layer of the synthesis network $g$ through a learned affine transform A, adds per-layer noise scaled by B, and starts the synthesis from a learned constant. Adapted from [@stylegan, Fig. 1].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-stylegan-arch.png){#fig-stylegan-arch width=100%}

### Structured noise injection: structured content at the input

SNI replaces the fixed input by a tensor assembled from location-specific mappings. A schematic form of its local/shared construction is [@sni, Secs. 3--4]

$$
X_0^{r}=\textcolor{blue}{P_r[z_r^{\mathrm{local}};z_{g(r)}^{\mathrm{region}};z^{\mathrm{global}}]+b_r},
\qquad (\gamma_\ell,\beta_\ell)=\textcolor{red}{L_\ell(f_s(z_s))}.
$$ {#eq-sni}

$r$ indexes input-grid cells and $g(r)$ their shared region. Separate $P_r$ restrict which local latent affects each cell. The paper's preferred configuration uses an $8\times8$ local grid, shared $2\times2$ region codes, and one global code; the lecture's $4\times4$ drawing is a simplified architecture, not its only setting. Style modulation begins later in the preferred configuration.

**Advantage:** local, regional, and global control without attribute labels. **Limitation:** content enters through the initial grid, while style can enter at many layers. Spatial leakage and remaining entanglement depend on grid/code design; changing background style may also change the foreground. The lecture calls this asymmetry the motivation for hierarchical DAT [@lecture-slides, p. 105].

### Diagonal GAN: hierarchical spatial gating

Diagonal GAN introduces content control at several resolutions alongside style control [@diagonal, Secs. 3--4; @lecture-slides, pp. 104--113]. With independent content and style latents, the paper's residual diagonal attention is

$$
\begin{aligned}
c&=f_c(z_c),\quad s=f_s(z_s),\quad d_\ell=\operatorname{sigmoid}(M_\ell(c)),\\
\textcolor{blue}{A_\ell(c)}&=I+\textcolor{blue}{\eta_\ell\operatorname{diag}(d_\ell)},\\
\widetilde X_\ell&=\textcolor{blue}{A_\ell(c)}X_\ell,
\qquad Y_\ell=\operatorname{AdaIN}(\widetilde X_\ell,\textcolor{red}{s}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-dat}

$\eta_\ell$ denotes the paper's learned coefficient $\beta$, renamed to avoid confusing it with AdaIN's shift. This is not dense query-key attention: every channel receives the same spatial gate. AdaIN's statistics are computed on its actual incoming tensor $\widetilde X_\ell$.

The paper also adds a diversity-sensitive term, often omitted by the slides:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DS}}=\mathbb{E}\left[
\textcolor{orange}{\max\{\tau-\|G(z_s,z_c^1)-G(z_s,z_c^2)\|_1,0\}}
\right],\qquad \mathcal{L}_G=\mathcal{L}_{G,\mathrm{adv}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DS}}.
$$ {#eq-dat-diversity}

The shared style is fixed while content varies. Once the distance exceeds $\tau$, this term stops rewarding further separation; it does **not** enforce a hard upper bound on the distance. Training uses non-saturating adversarial loss and $R_1$ discriminator regularization.

**Advantage:** spatial control at coarse and fine resolutions with $O(N)$ gate values. **Limitation:** a diagonal gate does not itself move pixels; geometric changes emerge through subsequent convolutions. Separation is an empirical inductive bias, not a theorem of perfect disentanglement.

![Where content enters, in the three generators of this section. (a) StyleGAN: the style code reaches every layer through the AdaIN boxes, each fed by its own affine transform A, while content arrives only as per-pixel noise scaled by the boxes B. (b) SNI: a separate content code enters once, as the input tensor. (c) Diagonal GAN: the content code reaches every layer as a diagonal attention map, which makes the content path symmetric with the style path. Adapted from [@diagonal, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-content-control.png){#fig-content-control width=100%}

![Where the two transforms act within one layer. The feature map is a cube of size $C \times H \times W$. The AdaIN parameters are a $C \times 1 \times 1$ vector, one scale and one shift per channel, applied identically at every pixel; the DAT attention map is a $1 \times H \times W$ map, one weight per pixel, applied identically to every channel. This is @eq-unified read one layer at a time. Adapted from [@lecture-slides].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-dat-adain-layer.png){#fig-dat-adain-layer width=100%}

 The lecture illustrates $4\times4$ pose/geometry, $8\times8$ expression, and finer eye/shape changes; these are examples rather than universal layer semantics.

### Generator-family comparison

| Model | Spatial/content input | Style mechanism | Distinctive change |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| StyleGAN | Shared learned constant; per-layer noise | Latent-predicted AdaIN | Per-resolution styles separate from stochastic detail |
| SNI | Local, regional, and global codes build the initial tensor | AdaIN | Structured content enters through the initial spatial tensor |
| Diagonal GAN | Content-predicted diagonal gates at multiple resolutions | AdaIN | Hierarchical spatial/content gating at several resolutions |

The progression in the lecture is therefore **constant + stochastic detail -> structured input -> hierarchical spatial gating**. The key limitation of ordinary StyleGAN noise is that independent noise mainly changes stochastic local detail rather than providing a stable semantic content control signal [@lecture-script]. SNI introduces structured spatial content but does so asymmetrically at the input; Diagonal GAN makes content control hierarchical, paralleling StyleGAN's multi-resolution style control.

## Paired and unpaired image translation {#sec-translation}

### Pix2Pix: realism plus paired reconstruction

Pix2Pix assumes aligned training pairs $(x,y)$. Its discriminator sees the input together with the proposed output, not the output alone [@pix2pix, Sec. 3; @lecture-slides, pp. 114--115]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cGAN}}(G,D)&=\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\log D(x,y)
+\mathbb{E}_{x,z}\log(1-D(x,G(x,z))),\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}&=\mathbb{E}_{x,y,z}\|y-G(x,z)\|_1,\\
G^*&=\arg\min_G\max_D\left[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cGAN}}+\textcolor{violet}{\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}}\right].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pix2pix}

The adversarial term tests conditional realism; the paired term anchors the output to the correct target. A U-Net generator preserves aligned structure through skip connections, and a PatchGAN discriminator checks local patches. The paper uses a non-saturating generator update in implementation and finds that explicit input noise tends to be ignored; dropout produces only modest variation.

**Advantage:** a shared conditional framework for many aligned translation tasks. **Limitation:** requires paired supervision and does not adequately represent all plausible outputs. It is **not unsupervised simply because it uses a GAN**.

![Image-to-image translation as one problem with many instances: in each case the same architecture and objective are trained on different paired data. Adapted from [@pix2pix, Fig. 1].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-i2i-tasks.png){#fig-i2i-tasks width=100%}

![The discriminator of a conditional GAN sees the input together with the output, which is what @eq-pix2pix means by $D(x,y)$. Left: a generated pair $(x, G(x))$ should be classified as fake. Right: a real pair $(x,y)$ should be classified as real. Adapted from [@pix2pix, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-pix2pix-cgan.png){#fig-pix2pix-cgan width=100%}

### Why unpaired translation is ill-posed

With unpaired collections, we observe marginals $p_{\mathcal{X}},p_{\mathcal{Y}}$, not the correspondence $p(x,y)$. Matching $G_\#p_{\mathcal{X}}=p_{\mathcal{Y}}$ does not tell us which target belongs to a particular input. For example, two equally likely inputs and two equally likely targets admit both possible bijections with exactly the same marginals. A constraint is necessary, but a constraint need not identify the intended semantics.

![Paired training data (left) consist of examples $\{x_i, y_i\}$ whose correspondence is known. Unpaired data (right) consist of a set $X$ and a set $Y$ with no information about which $x$ matches which $y$. Adapted from [@cyclegan, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-paired-unpaired.png){#fig-paired-unpaired width=100%}

![Why matching marginals is not enough, drawn for horses and zebras, with the pose of each animal standing for the content a translation should keep. (a) The correct mapping keeps the pose; (b) a shuffled mapping loses it. Both produce the same set of outputs, so a discriminator that sees only outputs has no reason to prefer (a) --- the argument of @sec-adv-illposed. Horse icon from Font Awesome Free, licensed under CC BY 4.0.](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-shuffled-mapping.png){#fig-shuffled-mapping width=100%}

### CycleGAN and the role of the cycle

CycleGAN uses $G:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$, $F:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$, and two discriminators [@cyclegan, Sec. 3; @lecture-slides, pp. 116--118]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}(G,D_Y)
&=\mathbb{E}_y\log D_Y(y)+\mathbb{E}_x\log(1-D_Y(G(x))),\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}
&=\mathbb{E}_x\|F(G(x))-x\|_1+\mathbb{E}_y\|G(F(y))-y\|_1,\\
\min_{G,F}\max_{D_X,D_Y}\quad
&\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}(G,D_Y)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}(F,D_X)
+\textcolor{violet}{\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-cyclegan}

The reverse adversarial term exchanges $x,y$ and $F,G$. The cycle compares a reconstructed image to its own input, so it needs no paired target in the other domain. The published implementation uses least-squares adversarial losses; the equation above is the paper's explanatory log-GAN formulation. An optional identity loss helps preserve appearance when an image is already in the target domain.

![The three parts of @eq-cyclegan. (a) Two mappings $G : X \to Y$ and $F : Y \to X$, each with its own discriminator. (b) Forward cycle consistency, $x \to G(x) \to F(G(x)) \approx x$. (c) Backward cycle consistency, $y \to F(y) \to G(F(y)) \approx y$. Adapted from [@cyclegan, Fig. 3].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-cyclegan-cycle.png){#fig-cyclegan-cycle width=100%}

**Advantage:** learns two-way translation from unpaired data.

![What unpaired translation produces, which the rest of this section
describes only as an objective. Each pair is a source image and the output of
a CycleGAN trained on two unpaired collections: photographs and Monet
paintings, horses and zebras, summer and winter. Note what changes and what
does not --- colour and texture are rewritten throughout, while the layout of
the scene and the pose of the animal survive, which is the bias
@sec-adv-cyclefail identifies as doing the real identification. Adapted from
[@cyclegan, Fig. 1].](figures/lec03/slides-cyclegan-results.png){#fig-cyclegan-results width=95%}

 **Limitation:** cycle consistency does not establish the correct semantic pairing, and optimization is substantially more delicate than in Pix2Pix. The lecture emphasizes the practical reason: CycleGAN jointly trains two generators and two discriminators, so adversarial objectives in both directions interact with the cycle term. In practice the networks are updated alternately rather than by solving a closed-form minimax problem; poorly balanced updates can produce unstable dynamics. This training difficulty was presented in class as an important hands-on lesson, not a minor implementation detail [@lecture-script]. @fig-translation contrasts paired supervision, round-trip reconstruction, domain-conditioned reconstruction, and style-code conditioning across the main translation models.

![Comparison of conditioning and supervision across image-to-image translation models. Pix2Pix uses a paired target $y$ to supervise $G(x)$; CycleGAN reconstructs the source after the round trip $x \to G(x) \to F(G(x))$; StarGAN reuses the same generator with the original domain label $k$ to reconstruct the source; and StarGAN v2 feeds both a source image $x$ and a target-domain style code $s_t$, where $s_t$ comes either from the mapping network $M_t(z)$ or the style encoder $E_t(x_{\mathrm{ref}})$.](figures/lec03/Jeongchan-Kim-translation.png){#fig-translation width=100%}

## Multiple domains and multiple inputs {#sec-multidomain}

The lecture presents a clear architectural progression. Pairwise CycleGAN/DiscoGAN-style translation scales poorly when every ordered domain pair needs its own mapping. StarGAN replaces those pairwise generators with one shared generator conditioned on a target domain label. StarGAN v2 then replaces the coarse label-only control with a compact, domain-specific style code that can be obtained from either a random latent or a reference image [@lecture-slides, pp. 119--125; @lecture-script].

### Scaling up: DiscoGAN and RadialGAN

For $K$ domains, separate directed pairwise generators require $K(K-1)$ maps: choose one source and one different target. This is a naive pairwise construction, not a universal lower bound. Slide 119 counts $K$ discriminators by sharing one per destination; independently trained CycleGAN pairs instead contain $K(K-1)$ discriminator instances.

![The counting argument of this section, drawn. (a) Translating among four domains with cross-domain models such as CycleGAN needs twelve generators, one for every ordered pair. (b) StarGAN serves five domains with a single generator that takes the target domain as an input. Adapted from [@stargan, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-stargan-star.png){#fig-stargan-star width=100%}

**DiscoGAN** independently develops bidirectional unpaired translation with adversarial losses and two reconstruction cycles [@discogan, Sec. 2]. In the present notation its generator objective has the structure

$$
\mathcal{L}_G=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}^{X\to Y}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}^{Y\to X}
+\textcolor{violet}{\lambda_X\mathbb{E}_x d(F(G(x)),x)
+\lambda_Y\mathbb{E}_y d(G(F(y)),y)}.
$$ {#eq-discogan}

$d$ is a reconstruction distance; the paper's illustration uses squared error. **Advantage:** discovers cross-domain relations without paired targets. **Limitation:** the basic formulation is two-domain, with the same correspondence ambiguity. It is related to CycleGAN, not necessarily identical in architecture or every loss detail.

**RadialGAN** routes domains through a shared latent space, with domain-specific encoders $E_i$ and decoders $G_j$ [@radialgan, Sec. 3]:

$$
u_i\ \xrightarrow{E_i}\ z\ \xrightarrow{G_j}\ \hat u_j,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{i}=
\mathbb{E}\|u_i-G_i(E_i(u_i))\|_2+
\mathbb{E}\|z-E_i(G_i(z))\|_2.
$$ {#eq-radialgan}

Here $u_i$ denotes a record including its response in the paper's continuous-response setting, and $z$ can come from other domains' encoders. Domain adversarial losses match translated and real records. **Advantage:** $O(K)$ encoder/decoder modules accommodate heterogeneous feature spaces. **Limitation:** requires a useful shared representation and still uses multiple domain modules. It is originally a predictive-data transfer method, not a many-image fusion model or a single universal generator like StarGAN.

### StarGAN: one generator conditioned on a domain label

StarGAN spatially replicates a target label $t$ and concatenates it with input $x$. Its discriminator has a real/fake output and an auxiliary domain classifier [@stargan, Sec. 3; @lecture-slides, pp. 120--122].

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{r}&=\mathbb{E}_{x,k}[-\log D_{\mathrm{cls}}(k\mid x)],\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{f}&=\mathbb{E}_{x,t}[-\log D_{\mathrm{cls}}(t\mid G(x,t))],\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}&=\mathbb{E}_{x,k,t}\|x-G(G(x,t),k)\|_1,\\
\mathcal{L}_D&=-\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{adv}}+\textcolor{teal}{\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{r}},\\
\mathcal{L}_G&=\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{adv}}+\textcolor{teal}{\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{f}}
+\textcolor{violet}{\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-stargan}

$\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{adv}}$ is the paper's log-GAN value in its explanatory formulation; its experiments replace this with WGAN-GP. Classification on real images trains $D$; classification on generated images trains $G$. The same $G$ is used twice for reconstruction. A dataset mask can indicate which labels are known when training jointly on datasets with different annotation sets.

**Advantage:** shares parameters across domains instead of training every pair separately. **Limitation:** the original deterministic mapping offers one output for fixed $(x,t)$ and needs domain labels. Label concatenation does not provide within-domain style diversity or fuse several source images.

![The four terms of @eq-stargan as training steps. (a) The discriminator learns to tell real from fake and to classify real images into their domains. (b) The generator takes the input image with the target domain label and produces a fake image. (c) The same generator maps that fake image back with the original label, which gives the reconstruction loss. (d) The generator learns to produce fakes the discriminator takes as real and classifies into the target domain. Adapted from [@stargan, Fig. 3].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-stargan-overview.png){#fig-stargan-overview width=100%}

### StarGAN v2: diverse, domain-specific style codes

StarGAN v2 replaces the fixed label input to $G$ with a style code injected through AdaIN. A mapping network $M_t(z)$ supplies latent-guided styles; a style encoder $E_t(x_{\mathrm{ref}})$ supplies reference-guided styles. $M$, $E$, and $D$ have domain-specific output heads, while $G$ is shared [@starganv2, Sec. 2; @lecture-slides, pp. 123--125].

$$
\textcolor{red}{s_t}=M_t(z)\ \text{or}\ E_t(x_{\mathrm{ref}}),\qquad
\hat x=G(x,\textcolor{red}{s_t}),\qquad s_k=E_k(x).
$$ {#eq-v2-inference}

Its key training terms, for $s_t^i=M_t(z_i)$, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{adv}}&=\mathbb{E}_{x,k}\log D_k(x)
+\mathbb{E}_{x,t,z}\log(1-D_t(G(x,s_t))),\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sty}}&=\mathbb{E}\|s_t-E_t(G(x,s_t))\|_1,\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ds}}&=\mathbb{E}\|G(x,s_t^1)-G(x,s_t^2)\|_1,\\
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}&=\mathbb{E}\|x-G(G(x,s_t),s_k)\|_1,\\
\min_{G,M,E}\max_D\quad &\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{adv}}
+\textcolor{red}{\lambda_{\mathrm{sty}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sty}}}
-\textcolor{orange}{\lambda_{\mathrm{ds}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ds}}}
+\textcolor{violet}{\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-starganv2}

Style reconstruction prevents ignoring the style input; the **minus** sign rewards different outputs; the cycle promotes source preservation. Unlike Diagonal GAN's thresholded diversity loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ds}}$ here is a distance reward. Recovering $s_t$ from a generated image does not force two unrelated latent- and reference-derived styles to be equal.

**Advantage:** latent and reference control with multiple outputs per target domain. **Limitation:** multiple objectives must balance diversity and preservation, and trained domains still need labels. The original model has neither a text encoder nor text cross-attention; the transcript's diffusion/text comparison is an analogy.

![The four modules of StarGAN v2. The generator translates an input image into an output reflecting a style code; the mapping network turns a latent code into style codes, one per domain; the style encoder extracts the style codes of a reference image; and the discriminator decides, for each domain, whether an image is a real image of that domain. All modules except the generator share their first layers and end in one branch per domain. Adapted from [@starganv2, Fig. 2].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-stargan-v2.png){#fig-starganv2-modules width=100%}

### Comparison at a glance

| Model | Input information | Added constraint or control | Main unresolved issue |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Pix2Pix | Paired $(x,y)$ | Paired $L_1$ reconstruction + conditional discriminator | Requires aligned pairs; limited multimodality |
| CycleGAN / DiscoGAN | Unpaired two-domain collections | Two adversarial directions + reconstruction cycle | Training stability and semantic ambiguity |
| RadialGAN | Heterogeneous domains | Shared latent + domain-specific encoders/decoders | Quality of the shared representation |
| StarGAN | One image + target domain label | Domain classification + shared-generator reconstruction | One output for fixed $(x,t)$ |
| StarGAN v2 | One image + latent/reference style | Style recovery + diversity + reconstruction | Diversity/preservation trade-off |

The main change from StarGAN to StarGAN v2 is not simply "more domains." StarGAN says **which target domain** is desired; StarGAN v2 additionally supplies **which style inside that domain**. This makes latent-guided and reference-guided multimodal outputs possible while keeping a single shared image generator.

**Training versus inference.** Discriminator updates treat generated images as detached samples. Generator updates propagate gradients through the discriminator while holding its parameters fixed; the cycle also backpropagates through the participating generators. Inference uses the trained generator and its required conditioning modules, not the discriminator. The distinction between a minimax value and the loss minimized by each optimizer is therefore important.

## Worked examples and reproducibility {#sec-examples}

### AdaIN with actual numbers

Take one content channel $u=(1,3)^\top$ and reference channel $v=(2,6)^\top$. Their means are $2,4$ and their population standard deviations are $1,2$. @eq-adain-def gives

$$
\operatorname{AdaIN}(u,v)=2(u-2\mathbf1)+4\mathbf1=(2,6)^\top.
$$

The transformed channel has the target mean and variance. It does not follow that the output image equals the style image: only these feature statistics were constrained.

### Matching marginals does not match correlations

Let $a=\sqrt2$ and choose centered two-channel feature matrices

$$
X=\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\-a&0\\0&a\\0&-a\end{bmatrix},\qquad
S=\begin{bmatrix}a&a/2\\-a&-a/2\\0&\sqrt{3/2}\\0&-\sqrt{3/2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then $\Sigma_X=I_2$ and $\Sigma_S=\begin{bmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{bmatrix}$. Both channels already have mean zero and standard deviation one. AdaIN therefore leaves $X$ unchanged and misses the target correlation. WCT multiplies $X$ by $\Sigma_S^{1/2}$ and obtains the requested covariance. This is a finite-dimensional counterexample to interpreting AdaIN as full covariance matching.

The following self-contained NumPy example verifies these claims; it is a mathematical check, not a GAN training experiment.

```{.python}
import numpy as np

def cov(x):
    xc = x - x.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    return xc.T @ xc / x.shape[0]

def spd_power(a, power):
    vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(a)
    if np.any(vals <= 0):
        raise ValueError("This example requires positive-definite covariance.")
    return (vecs * vals**power) @ vecs.T

a = np.sqrt(2.0)
x = np.array([[a, 0], [-a, 0], [0, a], [0, -a]])
s = np.array([[a, a/2], [-a, -a/2],
              [0, np.sqrt(1.5)], [0, -np.sqrt(1.5)]])
adain = (x - x.mean(0)) / x.std(0) * s.std(0) + s.mean(0)
wct = ((x - x.mean(0)) @ spd_power(cov(x), -0.5)
       @ spd_power(cov(s), 0.5) + s.mean(0))
assert np.allclose(cov(adain), np.eye(2))
assert np.allclose(cov(wct), cov(s))
print("AdaIN covariance:\n", np.round(cov(adain), 6))
print("WCT covariance:\n", np.round(cov(wct), 6))
```

## Connections and further reading {#sec-connections}

The lecture's central connection is between **where a representation is transformed** and **what a translation objective constrains**. Normalization/AdaIN act mainly on the channel axis, while spatial attention acts on the position axis; the unified $Y=AXT+B$ view makes this distinction explicit. StyleGAN, SNI, and Diagonal GAN then turn these transforms into architectural control signals at different resolutions. Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, StarGAN, and StarGAN v2 add progressively different kinds of supervision: paired targets, round-trip reconstruction, domain labels, and domain-specific style codes.

The main lecture should therefore be read as one progression rather than a list of GAN variants: **statistics -> axis-wise feature transforms -> controllable synthesis -> translation constraints -> scalable multi-domain conditioning**. The brief paper extensions above are useful related reading, but they are intentionally separated from the pp. 78--125/script narrative.

## Advanced topics {#sec-advanced-style}

The chapter above follows the lecture and its `Part 1 --- GAN` pages. This
section develops the points the lecture named and left, and the derivations
the main text states without giving. Each subsection is self-contained and
none is needed to follow the main line.

### Gram matrices, and why AdaIN is their diagonal case {#sec-adv-gram}

Before AdaIN, neural style transfer represented style by correlations of fixed encoder features. With $\Phi_\ell(I)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_\ell\times C_\ell}$ and $\Gamma_\ell(I)=\Phi_\ell(I)^\top\Phi_\ell(I)$, a representative objective is [@gatys]

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{style}}=
\sum_\ell a_\ell\|\Gamma_\ell(I_o)-\Gamma_\ell(I_s)\|_F^2,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{content}}=\|\Phi_{\ell_c}(I_o)-\Phi_{\ell_c}(I_c)\|_F^2.
$$ {#eq-gram-supp}

A Gram matrix is unchanged by a permutation of spatial positions, so it captures channel co-occurrence statistics more readily than layout. **Advantage:** rich multi-layer appearance matching. **Limitation:** the original method optimizes each output image iteratively and does not guarantee content preservation. AdaIN is a feed-forward statistic-matching alternative, not an exact solver of the Gram objective.

That is the statement. Why a Gram matrix is a representation of style at all,
and how it connects to the AdaIN the chapter has already used, is the part
worth spelling out.

Write $\Phi_\ell(I) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\ell \times C_\ell}$ for the features of
a frozen VGG layer, rows indexed by position and columns by channel. Then
$\Gamma_\ell = \Phi_\ell^\top \Phi_\ell$ has entries
$\Gamma_{cc'} = \sum_n \Phi_{nc}\Phi_{nc'}$: an uncentred second-order
statistic of the channels, summed over positions. Permuting the rows of
$\Phi_\ell$ leaves $\Gamma_\ell$ unchanged, which is the sense in which it
discards layout; what survives is *which channels fire together*, and for a
convolutional encoder a channel is a texture detector, so co-occurrence of
channels is texture. That is the whole argument, and it also bounds what the
representation can do: anything that depends on where the texture is placed is
invisible to it.

Which layer carries what is an empirical choice, and the usual one is that
content is read off a single deep layer --- `relu4_2` in Gatys et al. --- where
the representation is coarse enough to be insensitive to appearance, while
style is read off several layers at once, `relu1_1` through `relu5_1`, because
texture lives at every scale. The weights $a_\ell$ in @eq-gram-supp balance
them, and each layer's term is usually divided by $4 N_\ell^2 C_\ell^2$ so that
layers of different size contribute comparably.

The cost of the original method is the reason AdaIN exists. Gatys et al.
produce each output by *optimising the image*: start from noise or from the
content image and run L-BFGS on $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{content}} +
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{style}}$ for hundreds of iterations, each one a forward
and backward pass through VGG. Every new content-style pair pays this again.

Now the link. Take the diagonal of the Gram matrix and nothing else. Matching
$\Gamma_{cc}$ for every $c$ matches each channel's second moment, and matching
the feature means as well makes it each channel's mean and variance --- which
is exactly what @eq-adain-def does, in closed form, in one pass. AdaIN is
therefore the diagonal special case of Gram matching, computed rather than
optimised, and WCT of @eq-wct is the step that puts the off-diagonal entries
back. The three sit on one axis: diagonal second moments (AdaIN), full
covariance (WCT), full uncentred Gram across several layers (Gatys).

### The feed-forward form of style transfer {#sec-adv-adain-training}

@eq-adain-def is a transform, not a method: something has to turn the
transformed features back into an image. Huang and Belongie train a decoder
$g$ against a frozen VGG encoder $f$, and the two losses are worth writing out
because the first is not the obvious one.

With $t = \operatorname{AdaIN}(f(c), f(s))$ the target features and
$T = g(t)$ the output image,

$$
\mathcal{L}_c = \|f(T) - t\|_2 ,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_s = \sum_{\ell} \Big(
  \|\mu(\phi_\ell(T)) - \mu(\phi_\ell(s))\|_2
+ \|\sigma(\phi_\ell(T)) - \sigma(\phi_\ell(s))\|_2 \Big) ,
$$ {#eq-adain-losses}

minimising $\mathcal{L}_c + \lambda \mathcal{L}_s$ over the decoder alone. The
content loss is the distance to the *AdaIN output* $t$, not to $f(c)$: the
decoder is asked to reproduce the transformed features, not the original ones,
which is what lets a single decoder serve every style. The style loss matches
means and standard deviations across several VGG layers --- the diagonal
statistics of @sec-adv-gram, again --- rather than Gram matrices, and Huang and
Belongie report the two give comparable results at lower cost.

Because the transform is explicit, two knobs come for free at test time and
need no retraining. Interpolating $t$ towards $f(c)$,

$$
T_\alpha = g\big( (1-\alpha) f(c) + \alpha \operatorname{AdaIN}(f(c), f(s)) \big) ,
$$ {#eq-adain-alpha}

trades content against style continuously, with $\alpha = 0$ reconstructing the
content image. Interpolating between several styles' AdaIN targets mixes
styles. Neither is available to a decoder trained per style.

### Why the W space disentangles better than Z {#sec-adv-wspace}

The chapter answers this in one sentence --- the mapping can reshape the prior
--- and the standard account is worth the extra paragraph, because it explains
*what goes wrong* in $\mathcal{Z}$ rather than only what is better in
$\mathcal{W}$.

The prior on $\mathcal{Z}$ is fixed, $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$, and the
generator must push it onto the data distribution. Suppose some combination of
attributes is absent from the training data --- long hair together with a
masculine face, in the paper's example. The generator cannot map any region of
$\mathcal{Z}$ to that combination, so the map from $\mathcal{Z}$ to attributes
has to curve around the missing region. A curved map does not have axes: moving
along a straight line in $\mathcal{Z}$ changes several attributes at once,
which is entanglement, and it is forced by the shape of the data together with
the fixed shape of the prior.

$\mathcal{W}$ is under no distributional constraint at all. Nothing requires
$w = f(z)$ to be Gaussian, or to have any particular density, so the mapping
network can absorb the warping: $f$ takes the curvature and the synthesis
network sees a space in which the factors can be closer to axis-aligned.

![The curvature argument, drawn for two factors such as masculinity and hair length. Left: a training set in which one combination is missing. Middle: the map from $\mathcal{Z}$ to features must curve around the missing region, so a straight line in $\mathcal{Z}$ changes several factors at once. Right: the learned map from $\mathcal{Z}$ to $\mathcal{W}$ undoes much of that warping. Adapted from [@stylegan, Fig. 6].](figures/lec03/sbigstar0310-latent-warping.png){#fig-latent-warping width=100%}

 The
claim is that the warping has to happen somewhere and it is better done in a
learned space than forced into the generator.

Two measurements support it, and both deserve their definitions rather than
their names. **Perceptual path length** samples two latents, interpolates a
short step $\epsilon$ between them, and measures the perceptual distance
between the two images, averaged and normalised by $\epsilon^2$:

$$
\mathrm{PPL} = \mathbb{E}\left[ \tfrac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\,
  d_{\mathrm{VGG}}\big( G(\mathrm{lerp}(w_1,w_2;t)),\,
                        G(\mathrm{lerp}(w_1,w_2;t+\epsilon)) \big) \right] .
$$ {#eq-ppl}

A small value says the image changes at a steady rate along the path --- that
the latent space is not curved --- and it is the operational reading of
"less entangled". **Linear separability** is the complementary test: train an
auxiliary classifier on a binary attribute, then ask how well a *linear*
hyperplane in latent space separates the two classes, reported as a conditional
entropy. Both come out better for $\mathcal{W}$ than for $\mathcal{Z}$.

Two mechanisms in the paper follow directly. **Truncation** samples $w$ and
pulls it towards the mean, $w' = \bar{w} + \psi(w - \bar{w})$ with $\psi < 1$,
trading variety for quality; it is done in $\mathcal{W}$ precisely because
distances there are the perceptually meaningful ones. **Style mixing** draws
two codes and uses one before a randomly chosen layer and the other after,
during training, which stops the network from assuming that adjacent layers'
styles are correlated --- the regulariser that makes the per-resolution control
of @eq-stylegan actually hold.

### StyleGAN's noise, and what it is for {#sec-adv-noise}

The chapter defines $n_\ell$ correctly and asserts its role. The evidence is
an ablation, and it is worth stating because it is what separates *stochastic
variation* from *style* as the chapter uses the words.

The attributes the noise controls are the ones a viewer cannot name as
different: the exact placement of hair strands, freckles, skin pores, the
precise outline of the background. Resampling the noise with $w$ held fixed
changes all of these and changes nothing a human would call the person's
appearance. Removing the noise entirely does not give a cleaner image; it gives
a flat, painterly one, because the generator has no source of variation for
detail that ought to differ between samples and produces a featureless average
instead.

The scale experiment is what makes it an argument about architecture rather
than about texture. Noise fed only to the coarse layers moves large features
--- the overall curl of the hair; noise fed only to the fine layers moves only
the finest detail. So the noise inherits the resolution of the layer it enters,
exactly as the styles do in @eq-stylegan, and the two channels are independent:
$w$ sets what the image is, $n$ sets the arbitrary part of how it is realised.

### StyleGAN2: demodulation and path-length regularization {#sec-adv-stylegan2}

StyleGAN2 removes explicit instance normalization from the synthesis path and modulates/demodulates convolution weights [@stylegan2]. If $s_i$ is a style scale for input channel $i$,

$$
w'_{ijk}=\textcolor{red}{s_i}w_{ijk},\qquad
w''_{ijk}=\frac{w'_{ijk}}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i',k'}(w'_{i'jk'})^2+\epsilon}}.
$$ {#eq-stylegan2-supp}

Demodulation controls the expected output scale without normalizing each observed feature map, addressing the characteristic droplet artifacts associated with the original normalization design. StyleGAN2 also uses path-length regularization,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pl}}=
\mathbb{E}_{w,r}\left(\|J_g(w)^\top r\|_2-a\right)^2,
$$ {#eq-path-supp}

which encourages a more uniform sensitivity of the generated image to changes in $w$. **Advantage:** cleaner style modulation and fewer normalization artifacts. **Limitation:** these regularizers improve conditioning but do not guarantee semantic disentanglement.

Three points make the equations above an argument rather than a recipe.

*Where the droplet comes from.* Instance normalization standardises each
feature map after the convolution, which means a generator can put a very
large value in one spatial location and have the normalisation scale
everything else down around it. The strong local signal survives, because it
is what sets the scale; the rest of the map is suppressed. That is the droplet
--- a blob-shaped artefact that appears in the feature maps from $64\times64$
onwards and, once the network depends on it, in the output. Removing
normalisation from the forward path removes the mechanism.

*Why dividing by that particular norm works.* Suppose the inputs to the
convolution are independent with unit variance. After modulation the output
$j$ has variance $\sum_{i,k}(w'_{ijk})^{2}$, so dividing the weights by
$\sqrt{\sum_{i',k'}(w'_{i'jk'})^{2}}$ restores unit output variance. The
essential difference from instance normalization is the object being
normalised: this acts on the **weights**, using the *expected* statistics
under an assumption about the input, and not on the observed feature map. The
generator therefore has no observed quantity to game, which is why the droplet
does not come back.

*The regulariser and its metric.* In @eq-path-supp the constant $a$ is not a
hyperparameter but a running exponential average of the observed
$\|J_g(w)^\top r\|_2$, so the term penalises deviation from the network's own
current average sensitivity rather than from a chosen value. Its cost is a
Jacobian-vector product, so it is applied *lazily*, once every 16 minibatches,
with the step size scaled accordingly. And it is the same quantity the
perceptual path length of @eq-ppl measures: StyleGAN2 regularises the metric
that StyleGAN introduced to diagnose entanglement, which is why the two move
together. StyleGAN2 also drops progressive growing, whose phase-in of new
resolutions left a preference for fixed detail locations, in favour of skip
and residual connections that train at full resolution throughout.

### The solution set of unpaired translation {#sec-adv-illposed}

The chapter's two-point example shows that two bijections match the marginals.
The situation is worse than "two", and saying how much worse is what justifies
everything that follows it.

Let $G$ satisfy $G_{\#}p_{\mathcal{X}} = p_{\mathcal{Y}}$ and let $\tau$ be any
measure-preserving automorphism of $(\mathcal{Y}, p_{\mathcal{Y}})$, that is,
any map with $\tau_{\#}p_{\mathcal{Y}} = p_{\mathcal{Y}}$. Then

$$
(\tau \circ G)_{\#} p_{\mathcal{X}}
  = \tau_{\#}\big( G_{\#} p_{\mathcal{X}} \big)
  = \tau_{\#} p_{\mathcal{Y}} = p_{\mathcal{Y}} ,
$$ {#eq-illposed}

so $\tau \circ G$ is just as valid. For a continuous $p_{\mathcal{Y}}$ the
group of such $\tau$ is infinite-dimensional, so the adversarial objective
alone picks out nothing: its solution set is an orbit, not a point.

Cycle consistency shrinks the set but does not collapse it. Requiring
$F \circ G \approx \mathrm{id}$ forces $G$ to be approximately invertible,
which removes the $\tau$ that destroy information; it does not remove the ones
that are themselves invertible, and a swap of two equally likely modes is
invertible. So what actually identifies the intended map is neither term. It is
the architecture: a residual convolutional generator with a receptive field
much smaller than the image, trained from an identity-like initialisation,
finds small, local, low-frequency changes far more easily than a global
rearrangement. The inductive bias is doing the identification, which is why the
failures in @sec-adv-cyclefail are the ones they are.

### How cycle consistency fails {#sec-adv-cyclefail}

Two failures are named in the chapter. Both are worth developing, because each
is a consequence of the objective rather than an accident of training.

**Steganography.** Chu et al. showed that a CycleGAN trained on aerial
photographs and maps reconstructs features of the source that are not visible
in the intermediate image at all: a building absent from the generated map
reappears in the reconstruction. The generator has learned to encode the source
in a low-amplitude, high-frequency signal that the map-domain discriminator
cannot see and the reverse generator can read. The cycle loss is then near
zero while the intermediate image is semantically wrong --- the objective is
satisfied and the task is not.

The mechanism follows from what is penalised. The cycle term constrains the
*composition* $F \circ G$, not $G$ alone, so any information channel that
survives the round trip is rewarded, whether or not it is part of the visible
translation. Adding noise to the intermediate image, or otherwise destroying the
high-frequency channel, degrades the reconstruction sharply --- which is the
test that distinguishes hidden information from honest translation.

**Geometry.** The original CycleGAN paper reports the limitation plainly:
tasks requiring shape change fail while tasks requiring texture change succeed.
Apple to orange keeps the apple's outline and repaints it; horse to zebra
paints stripes on the horse, and on a rider as well if one is present, because
nothing in the objective knows that a rider is not a horse; dog to cat produces
minimal change. The reason is the same inductive bias as in @sec-adv-illposed,
read the other way: a residual convolutional generator is well suited to
recolouring a pixel from its neighbourhood and badly suited to moving content
across the image, and a PatchGAN discriminator judges local patches, so it
scores texture and is largely blind to global shape. Neither network is asked
for geometry and neither provides it.

### OT-driven CycleGAN and CycleGAN failure modes {#sec-adv-otcycle}

A related optimal-transport formulation derives CycleGAN rather than modifying it [@otcycle]. It is worth following the direction of that derivation, because it answers the question the lecture leaves open --- where the cycle term comes from --- and the answer is the opposite of what the shape of the objective suggests.

Start from a Kantorovich problem between the two domains, with a *joint* transport cost that charges a pair $(x,y)$ for the round trip under the two maps $R:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$ and $H:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$,

$$
d\big((x,y)\big)=\|x-R(y)\|+\|y-H(x)\|.
$$ {#eq-otcycle-cost}

Minimising $\int d \, d\pi$ over couplings $\pi$ of $p_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $p_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is the primal problem, and its objective **is** the cycle/data-consistency term: @eq-otcycle-cost is what $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}$ measures. The marginal constraints are then relaxed by Kantorovich duality, and it is the *dual* of those constraints that produces two Wasserstein-1 terms, each realised by a 1-Lipschitz critic. Collecting the two,

$$
\min_{R,H}
\textcolor{violet}{\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}(R,H)}
+W_1(p_{\mathcal X},R_\#p_{\mathcal Y})+
W_1(p_{\mathcal Y},H_\#p_{\mathcal X}).
$$ {#eq-otcycle-supp}

So the reading to carry away is not "$W_1$ matching, plus a cycle penalty of unexplained origin". It is: **the cycle term is the transport cost, and the adversarial terms are the penalties that enforce the marginals.** The weight $\lambda$ is the exchange rate between the two, and taking $\lambda$ large is what recovers the hard marginal constraints of the original Kantorovich problem. The critics are 1-Lipschitz because that is what the dual asks for, not because a Lipschitz constraint was found to stabilise training.

This remains a **surrogate training objective** once the ideal critic class is replaced by neural networks, so the equality between theory and implementation should not be overstated.

Cycle consistency also has important failure modes. First, it does not identify the intended semantic pairing: two domains with two equally likely elements admit a swapped bijection with perfect marginal matching and zero cycle error. Second, a network can hide source information in visually weak high-frequency signals and use it to reconstruct the input, producing a small cycle loss without meaningful visible preservation [@steganography]. Large geometric changes were also reported as difficult in the original CycleGAN study [@cyclegan]. Thus realistic marginals plus a small cycle loss are not a certificate of correct correspondence.

### StarGAN's mask vector {#sec-adv-mask}

The chapter mentions the mask in a clause. It is what lets one generator train
on two datasets whose label sets do not overlap --- CelebA with facial
attributes, RaFD with expressions --- and the encoding is simple enough to give
in full.

The label fed to the generator is a concatenation
$\tilde{c} = [c_1, \dots, c_n, m]$, where $c_i$ is the label vector for dataset
$i$ and $m$ is a one-hot mask naming which dataset the current example came
from. The entries of every $c_i$ but the active one are set to zero and are to
be ignored. The generator learns to read $m$ and attend to the corresponding
block, so a CelebA example carries expression bits that are zero and
uninformative rather than zero and meaningful.

The discriminator's classification head is split to match: it predicts labels
for both datasets, and the classification loss for an example is computed only
over the head belonging to its own dataset. Without the mask the zeros would be
indistinguishable from genuine negative labels, and the generator would learn
that every CelebA face has a neutral expression.

### CollaGAN: many inputs, one output {#sec-adv-collagan}

CollaGAN considers a different data regime from StarGAN: several **corresponding** domain observations of the same subject are available and one target domain is missing [@collagan]. With target domain $t$ withheld,

$$
\hat x_t=G(\textcolor{blue}{\{x_j:j\ne t\}},t),\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mcyc}}=
\mathbb{E}_t\sum_{j\ne t}\|x_j-\tilde x_{j\mid t}\|_1.
$$ {#eq-collagan-supp}

The multiple-cycle construction reconstructs each available input after inserting the predicted missing image. **Advantage:** it can fuse complementary observations from several domains. **Limitation:** it requires corresponding multi-domain input sets, so it solves a different problem from single-input unpaired translation.

That is the summary. The setting deserves more, because it is the one where
this lab's own work sits and because the objective is not a relabelling of
StarGAN's.

The problem is imputation with several co-registered observations: $N$ MR
contrasts of the same slice, one of which is missing. A single-input
translation model must pick one available contrast and discard the rest.
CollaGAN takes all of them, so the generator is a map
$G(\{x_i\}_{i \ne t}, t) \mapsto \hat{x}_t$, from every available input plus a
target index to the missing one.

Cycle consistency has to be rebuilt for that signature, and the two-step form
is the point of the paper. Having produced $\hat{x}_t$, put it back into the
input set in place of the real $x_t$ and ask for some *other* contrast $j$:

$$
\tilde{x}_{j \mid t}
  = G\big( \{\hat{x}_t\} \cup \{x_i : i \ne t, j\},\; j \big) ,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mcc}} = \sum_{j \ne t} \big\| x_j - \tilde{x}_{j \mid t} \big\|_1 .
$$ {#eq-collagan-cycle}

A single round trip would only check that $\hat{x}_t$ is invertible back to
where it came from; this *multiple* cycle checks that it is consistent with
every other contrast at once, which is what a wrong but plausible $\hat{x}_t$
fails. The discriminator carries a classification head over contrasts, as in
@eq-stargan, so the output must also be recognisable as contrast $t$. For MR
synthesis the reconstruction term is supplemented by a structural-similarity
term, since $L_1$ alone tolerates the loss of fine structure that matters
clinically.

The reason the collaborative version wins is worth stating plainly: the
contrasts are different measurements of the same anatomy, so what is missing
from one is usually present in another. A model that reads only one of them
throws away exactly the redundancy the problem provides.
